meta.title: Who really said "Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics. Universities won't survive"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Peter Drucker said it, to Forbes on 10 March 1997. The thirty-year clock runs to 2027. Verified against the original interview and Quote Investigator.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics. Universities won't survive'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine, and verbatim. Peter Drucker told Forbes this on 10 March 1997 — which fixes the deadline of his prediction at 2027, not whenever you read it.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Drucker said it to Forbes in a long interview at Claremont, California published on 10 March 1997 under the title “Seeing things as they really are.” The wording that circulates is verbatim — though most retellings stop before the third sentence, “It’s as large a change as when we first got the printed book.”

source.excerpt: Drucker says the current setup is doomed, at least so far as higher education is concerned. “Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics. Universities won’t survive. It’s as large a change as when we first got the printed book.”
trail: The line sits on page 7 of a nine-page Forbes interview published 10 March 1997 ↗, bylined Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson, immediately after the writers note that Drucker thinks the current setup is doomed so far as higher education is concerned.

Quote Investigator ↗ traced the quotation to that same interview and concluded that Drucker did deliver it, adding that the two interviewers flew to Claremont, California and spent ten hours speaking with him about the future.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the full three-sentence quotation in its sourced “1990s and later” section, citing the same Forbes article and date.
A 2005 Internet Archive capture of the page ↗ shows the wording, the byline and the 03.10.97 dateline exactly as first published online.
source.excerptNote: From page 7 of 9 of the online Forbes interview, in the section on education. The first sentence is the interviewers’ framing, not Drucker’s; the original leaves the quotation open at the end of the paragraph and continues it into his remarks on the cost of college.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: About Peter Drucker
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-American writer on management · Claremont Graduate University
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker was born in Vienna in 1909, naturalised as an American citizen in 1943, and died in 2005. More than anyone else he turned management into a subject you could study rather than merely practise, writing prolifically across six decades and teaching at Claremont Graduate University from 1971 until the end of his life. In 1997 two Forbes writers flew out to Claremont and spent ten hours asking him what the next thirty years would look like; higher education was one of his answers.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound, which makes this quote unusual: everything that goes wrong with it happens after the name is already correct.

items.why: The short version travels much better than the real one. The reader who wrote in to Quote Investigator ↗ arrived with only that fragment and no idea where it came from. The full sentence carries a date, a scale and a comparison — the arrival of the printed book — that the stub throws away.

items.who: Retellings that restart the thirty-year clock
items.why: “Thirty years from now” was said in March 1997, which fixes the horizon at 2027 — Quote Investigator ↗ states this outright. Quoted in a later decade without its date, the sentence reads as a fresh forecast rather than one whose term is very nearly up.

items.scope: Two Forbes pieces, three months apart
items.who: A second, genuinely different Drucker line
items.why: Forbes ran him again on 16 June 1997 in “I got my degree through E-mail” ↗, quoting him as saying: “Universities won’t survive. The future is outside the traditional campus, outside the traditional classroom. Distance learning is coming on fast.” Both lines are real, but they are not the same quotation, and the campuses-as-relics wording belongs only to the March interview.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine, and verbatim. Drucker said it to Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson for Forbes, 10 March 1997 ↗. The only correction worth making is to the calendar.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Drucker was not really making a technology prophecy. He was making a cost argument. In the same interview he pointed out that the cost of higher education had risen as fast as the cost of health care, while for the middle-class family a college education for their children had become “as much of a necessity as is medical care.” That combination — runaway price with no visible improvement in the content or the quality of the education — was what he called rapidly becoming untenable.

The delivery mechanism he imagined was the one available in 1997. “Already we are beginning to deliver more lectures and classes off campus via satellite or two-way video at a fraction of the cost,” he told Forbes, concluding that today’s campus buildings were “hopelessly unsuited and totally unneeded.” Reviewing the same passage in 2011, The New Republic noted that the big universities were instead bigger and, after a stellar year for endowment investments, richer than almost ever before.
detailsBody: Drucker spoke at Claremont, California, where he had taught since 1971; Quote Investigator records that the two interviewers spent ten hours with him. He died in 2005, and so will not see whether the 2027 deadline holds.
context.pull: The prediction has a deadline, not a mood — the thirty years run to 2027.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Peter Drucker delivered the quotation in a 1997 Forbes interview titled "Seeing things as they really are" by Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson, that the interviewers flew to Claremont and spent ten hours with him, and that the thirty-year prediction runs until 2027.

The live Forbes page for "Seeing things as they really are" (Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson, March 10, 1997) contains the quotation about university campuses becoming relics, plus the lines about the printed book and campus buildings being "hopelessly unsuited and totally unneeded".

A 2005 Internet Archive capture of page 7 of 9 of the Forbes article reproduces verbatim: "Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics. Universities won't survive. It's as large a change as when we first got the printed book." — under the byline Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson, Forbes Magazine, 03.10.97, preceded by the writers' framing that Drucker says the current setup is doomed so far as higher education is concerned.

Wikiquote's Peter Drucker page carries the full quotation in its sourced "1990s and later" section, cited to "Seeing things as they really are", Forbes (March 10, 1997), and separately lists the June 16, 1997 Forbes line.
Kevin Carey's New Republic article of November 17, 2011 quotes the full Drucker prediction and observes that the big universities had instead become bigger and richer than almost ever before.

The Forbes article "I got my degree through E-mail" (June 16, 1997) quotes Drucker separately as saying: "Universities won't survive. The future is outside the traditional campus, outside the traditional classroom. Distance learning is coming on fast."

Peter Drucker was born 19 November 1909 in Vienna, died 11 November 2005, was naturalised as a US citizen in 1943, and taught at Claremont Graduate University from 1971 to 2005; he was a management consultant, educator and author.
